blocks.p: God, sitting on his throne, sees Satan flying toward this world, then newly created, and points him out to the Son, who sits at his right hand. He foretells that Satan will succeed in perverting mankind, and clears his own justice and wisdom of all blame, since he created Man free and strong enough to have withstood his tempter; yet he declares his purpose of grace toward Man, because Man did not fall through his own malice, as Satan did, but was led astray by Satan. The Son of God praises his Father for revealing this gracious purpose toward Man. God declares again that grace cannot be extended to Man unless divine justice is satisfied: Man has offended the majesty of God by aspiring to godhead, and therefore, with all his descendants, he is condemned to death and must die, unless someone can be found able to answer for his offense and undergo his punishment. The Son of God freely offers himself as a ransom for Man. The Father accepts him, ordains his incarnation, proclaims his exaltation above all in Heaven and Earth, and commands all the angels to worship him. They obey, and, singing to their harps in full choir, celebrate the Father and the Son. Meanwhile Satan lands on the bare outer shell of this world’s outermost sphere. Wandering there, he first finds a place since called the Limbo of Vanity; the poem tells what persons and things fly up to it. From there he comes to the gate of Heaven, which is described, with the stairs that ascend to it and the waters above the firmament that flow around it. He passes on to the orb of the Sun and finds Uriel there, the regent of that orb; but first he changes himself into the shape of a lesser angel. Pretending a zealous wish to see the new creation and Man, whom God had placed in it, he asks Uriel where Man lives, and is directed there. He lands first on Mount Niphates.

v: Hail, holy Light, offspring of Heaven firstborn,
Or the Eternal’s co-eternal beam,
May I say this unblamed? Since God is light,
And never but in light no one could reach
Dwelt from eternity, dwelt then in you,
Bright outflow of bright essence, uncreated.
Or would you rather be called pure heavenly stream,
Whose fountain who can tell? Before the sun,
Before the heavens you were, and at the voice
Of God, as with a mantle, you arrayed
The rising world of waters dark and deep,
Won from the void and formless infinite.
You I revisit now with bolder wing,
Escaped the Stygian pool, though long detained
In that obscure abode, while in my flight
Through utter and through middle darkness borne
With other notes than to the Orphic lyre
I sang of Chaos and eternal Night,
Taught by the heavenly Muse to venture down
The dark descent, and up to climb again,
Though hard and rare. You I revisit safe,
And feel your sovereign, vital lamp; but you
Do not come back to eyes that roll in vain
To find your piercing ray, and find no dawn;
So thick a drop serene has quenched their orbs,
Or dim suffusion veiled. And yet no less
Do I still wander where the Muses haunt
Clear spring, or shady grove, or sunny hill,
Struck with the love of sacred song; but most
You, Zion, and the flowery brooks beneath
That wash your hallowed feet and warbling flow,
I visit nightly, and at times recall
Those other two who share with me my fate,
If only I could equal their renown,
Blind Thamyris and blind Maeonides,
Tiresias and Phineus, seers of old.
Then feed on thoughts that of their own will stir
Harmonious numbers, as the wakeful bird
Sings in the dark, and, hidden in deepest shade,
Tunes her nocturnal note. So with the year
Seasons return, but never to me returns
Day, or the sweet approach of dusk or dawn,
Or sight of springtime bloom, or summer’s rose,
Or flocks, or herds, or human face divine;
But cloud instead, and never-ending dark
Surrounds me, from the cheerful ways of men
Cut off, and for the lovely book of knowledge
Presented with a universal blank
Of Nature’s works, for me wiped out, erased,
And wisdom at one entrance quite shut out.
So much the more, then, you, celestial Light,
Shine inward, and the mind through all her powers
Illumine; plant eyes there; all mist from there
Purge and disperse, that I may see and tell
Of things invisible to mortal sight.
Now the Almighty Father from above,
From the pure Empyrean where he sits
Throned high above all height, bent down his eye
To view his own works and their works at once.
Around him all the holy ones of Heaven
Stood thick as stars, and from his sight received
Bliss beyond utterance; and on his right
The radiant image of his glory sat,
His only Son. On Earth he first beheld
Our two first parents, still the only two
Of mankind, in the happy Garden placed,
Reaping immortal fruits of joy and love,
Uninterrupted joy, unrivaled love,
In blissful solitude. He then surveyed
Hell and the gulf between, and Satan there
Coasting the wall of Heaven on this side Night,
High in the dusky air, and ready now
To drop with weary wings and willing feet
On the bare outside of this world, that seemed
Firm land surrounded, with no sky above,
Uncertain which, by ocean or by air.
God, watching him from his high vantage point,
From which he sees past, present, future, all,
Spoke thus, foreseeing, to his only Son:
“Only begotten Son, you see what rage
Transports our adversary, whom no bounds
Prescribed, no bars of Hell, nor all the chains
Heaped on him there, nor yet the vast Abyss
Gaping between, can hold; so bent he seems
On desperate revenge, that will rebound
Upon his own rebellious head. And now,
Breaking through all restraint, he wings his way
Not far from Heaven, in the precincts of light,
Directly toward the new-created world,
And Man placed there, intending now to test
If he by force can ruin him, or, worse,
Pervert by some false guile; and will pervert;
For man will listen to his flattering lies,
And easily transgress the sole command,
Sole pledge of his obedience. So will fall
He and his faithless progeny. Whose fault?
Whose but his own? Ingrate, he had from me
All he could have; I made him just and right,
Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall.
So I created all the heavenly Powers
And Spirits, those who stood and those who failed;
Freely they stood who stood, and fell who fell.
Not free, what proof could they have given, sincere,
Of true allegiance, constant faith or love,
Where only what they had to do appeared,
Not what they would? What praise could they receive?
What pleasure I, from such obedience paid,
When will and reason (reason also is choice),
Useless and empty, both of freedom stripped,
Made passive both, had served necessity,
Not me? They therefore, as by right was due,
Were so created, nor can justly blame
Their maker, or their making, or their fate,
As if predestination overruled
Their will, disposed by absolute decree
Or high foreknowledge. They themselves decreed
Their own revolt, not I. If I foreknew,
Foreknowledge had no influence on their fault,
Which, unforeknown, would have been no less sure.
So without least impulse or shade of fate,
Or anything I changelessly foresaw,
They trespass, authors to themselves in all,
Both what they judge and what they choose; for so
I formed them free, and free they must remain
Till they enslave themselves; or I must change
Their nature, and revoke the high decree,
Unchangeable, eternal, which ordained
Their freedom; they themselves ordained their fall.
The first sort by their own suggestion fell,
Self-tempted, self-depraved; Man falls deceived
By the other first. Man therefore shall find grace,
The other none. In mercy and justice both,
Through Heaven and Earth, so shall my glory excel,
But mercy first and last shall brightest shine.”
While God spoke thus, ambrosial fragrance filled
All Heaven, and in the blessed, chosen spirits
Spread a new joy too deep for any words.
Beyond compare the Son of God was seen
Most glorious; in him all his Father shone
Substantially expressed, and in his face
Divine compassion visibly appeared,
Love without end, and grace beyond all measure;
And, voicing these, he spoke so to his Father:
“O Father, gracious was that word which closed
Your sovereign sentence, that Man should find grace;
For which both Heaven and Earth shall lift on high
Your praises, with the countless, mighty sound
Of hymns and sacred songs, with which your throne,
Encircled, shall proclaim you ever blessed.
For should Man finally be lost, should Man,
Your creature, lately so loved, your youngest son,
Fall, circumvented thus by fraud, though joined
With his own folly? Be that far from you,
Far be that from you, Father, who are judge
Of all things made, and judge with right alone.
Or shall the adversary thus obtain
His end, and frustrate yours? Shall he fulfill
His malice, and your goodness bring to nothing,
Or go back proud, though to a heavier doom,
Yet with revenge accomplished, and to Hell
Drag after him the whole race of mankind,
By him corrupted? Or will you yourself
Abolish your creation, and unmake,
For him, what for your glory you have made?
So would your goodness and your greatness both
Be questioned and blasphemed without defense.”
To whom the great Creator thus replied:
“O Son, in whom my soul has chief delight,
Son of my bosom, Son who are alone
My word, my wisdom, and effectual might,
All you have said is as my thoughts are, all
As my eternal purpose has decreed.
Man shall not quite be lost, but saved who will,
Yet not of will in him, but grace in me
Freely bestowed. Once more I will renew
His lapsed powers, though forfeit and enslaved
By sin to foul, exorbitant desires;
Upheld by me, yet once more he shall stand
On even ground against his mortal foe,
By me upheld, that he may know how frail
His fallen state is, and to me may owe
All his deliverance, and to none but me.
Some I have chosen by a special grace,
Elect above the rest; so is my will.
The rest shall hear me call, be often warned
Of their sinful state, and to appease in time
The angry Deity, while offered grace
Invites; for I will clear their darkened senses
Enough to serve, and soften stony hearts
To pray, repent, and bring obedience due.
To prayer, repentance, and obedience due,
Though only tried, if with sincere intent,
My ear shall not be slow, my eye not shut.
And I will place within them as a guide
My umpire Conscience, whom if they will hear,
Light after light, well used, they shall attain,
And, to the end persisting, safe arrive.
This long forbearance and my day of grace
Those who neglect and scorn shall never taste;
But hard be hardened, blind be blinded more,
That they may stumble on, and deeper fall;
And none but such from mercy I exclude.
But yet all is not done. Man, disobeying,
Disloyal, breaks his fealty, and sins
Against the high supremacy of Heaven,
Grasping at godhead, and so losing all,
To expiate his treason has nothing left,
But, set apart, devoted to destruction,
He with his whole posterity must die,
Die he or Justice must; unless for him
Some other, able and as willing, pay
The rigid satisfaction, death for death.
Say, heavenly Powers, where shall we find such love?
Which of you will be mortal to redeem
Man’s mortal crime, and, just, save the unjust?
Dwells in all Heaven a love so dear as that?”
He asked, but all the heavenly choir stood mute,
And silence was in Heaven. On man’s behalf
No patron or intercessor appeared,
Much less one who dared draw on his own head
The deadly forfeit, and set down the ransom.
And now, without redemption, all mankind
Must have been lost, condemned to Death and Hell
By sentence severe, had not the Son of God,
In whom the fullness dwells of love divine,
Renewed his dearest mediation thus:
“Father, your word is passed: man shall find grace;
And shall not grace find means, who finds her way,
The swiftest of your winged messengers,
To visit all your creatures, and to all
Comes unprevented, unimplored, unsought?
Happy for man, so coming; for her aid
He never can seek, once dead in sins and lost;
Atonement for himself, or offering fit,
Indebted and undone, has none to bring.
Behold me, then: me for him, life for life
I offer; on me let your anger fall;
Account me man; I for his sake will leave
Your bosom, and this glory next to you
Freely put off, and for him lastly die
Well pleased; on me let Death wreak all his rage.
Under his gloomy power I shall not long
Lie vanquished; you have given me to possess
Life in myself forever; by you I live,
Though now to Death I yield, and am his due,
All that of me can die; yet, that debt paid,
You will not leave me in the loathsome grave
His prey, nor will you let my spotless soul
Forever with corruption there to dwell;
But I shall rise victorious, and subdue
My vanquisher, stripped of his boasted spoil;
Death shall receive his own death’s wound, and stoop
Inglorious, of his mortal sting disarmed.
I through the ample air in triumph high
Shall lead Hell captive, spite of Hell, and show
The powers of darkness bound. You, at the sight
Pleased, out of Heaven shall look down and smile,
While, raised by you, I ruin all my foes,
Death last, and with his carcass glut the grave.
Then I, with all the multitude redeemed,
Shall enter Heaven, long absent, and return,
Father, to see your face, in which no cloud
Of anger shall remain, but peace assured
And reconcilement; wrath shall be no more
Henceforth, but in your presence perfect joy.”
His words here ended, but his gentle look
Silent yet spoke, and breathed immortal love
To mortal men, above which only shone
Filial obedience: as a sacrifice
Glad to be offered, he awaits the will
Of his great Father. Utter wonder seized
All Heaven, what this might mean, and where it led,
They pondered; but the Almighty soon replied:
“O you in Heaven and Earth the only peace
Found out for mankind under wrath, O you
My one delight! You know full well how dear
To me are all my works, nor Man the least,
Though last created, that for him I spare
You from my bosom and right hand, to save,
By losing you a while, the whole race lost.
Therefore, of those you only can redeem
Unite their nature also with your own;
And be yourself Man among men on Earth,
Made flesh, when time shall be, of virgin seed,
By wondrous birth; be you in Adam’s place
The head of all mankind, though Adam’s son.
As in him all men perish, so in you,
As from a second root, shall be restored
As many as are restored; without you, none.
His crime makes guilty all his sons; your merit,
Imputed, shall absolve those who renounce
Their own deeds, righteous and unrighteous both,
And live in you transplanted, and from you
Receive new life. So Man, as is most just,
Shall satisfy for Man, be judged and die,
And dying rise, and rising with him raise
His brothers, ransomed with his own dear life.
So heavenly love shall outdo hellish hate,
Giving to death, and dying to redeem,
So dearly to redeem what hellish hate
So easily destroyed, and still destroys
In those who, when they may, refuse the grace.
Nor shall you, by descending to assume
Man’s nature, lessen or degrade your own.
Because you have, though throned in highest bliss,
Equal to God, and equally enjoying
Godlike delight, left everything to save
A world from utter loss, and have been found
By merit more than birthright Son of God,
Found worthiest to be so by being good,
Far more than great or high; because in you
Love has abounded more than glory abounds,
Therefore your humiliation shall exalt
With you your manhood also to this throne;
Here you shall sit incarnate, here shall reign
Both God and Man, Son both of God and Man,
Anointed universal King. All power
I give you; reign forever, and assume
Your merits; under you, as Head supreme,
Thrones, Princedoms, Powers, Dominions I subject:
All knees shall bow to you, of those who live
In Heaven, or Earth, or under Earth in Hell,
When you, attended gloriously from Heaven,
Appear in the sky, and from your presence send
The summoning archangels to proclaim
Your dread tribunal; at once from all the winds
The living, and at once the summoned dead
Of all past ages, to the general doom
Shall hasten; such a peal shall rouse their sleep.
Then, all your saints assembled, you shall judge
Bad men and angels; they, arraigned, shall sink
Beneath your sentence; Hell, her numbers full,
Henceforth shall be forever shut. Meanwhile
The world shall burn, and from her ashes spring
New Heaven and Earth, in which the just shall dwell,
And after all their long tribulations
See golden days, fruitful of golden deeds,
With joy and love triumphing, and fair truth.
Then you shall lay your royal scepter by,
Since then no royal scepter shall be needed;
God shall be all in all. But all you gods,
Adore him, dying to achieve all this;
Adore the Son, and honor him as me.”
No sooner had the Almighty ceased than all
The multitude of angels, with a shout
Loud as from numbers without number, sweet
As from blest voices, uttering joy, Heaven rang
With jubilee, and loud hosannas filled
The eternal regions. Lowly, reverent,
Toward either throne they bow, and to the ground
With solemn adoration down they cast
Their crowns, woven with amaranth and gold,
Immortal amaranth, a flower which once
In Paradise, close by the Tree of Life,
Began to bloom, but soon, for man’s offense,
To Heaven was moved, where first it grew; there grows,
And flowers aloft, shading the Fount of Life,
And where the river of bliss through Heaven’s midst
Rolls over Elysian flowers her amber stream.
With these that never fade the Spirits elect
Bind their resplendent locks, entwined with beams.
Now, in loose garlands thick thrown off, the bright
Pavement, that like a sea of jasper shone,
Empurpled with celestial roses, smiled.
Then, crowned again, their golden harps they took,
Harps ever tuned, that, glittering by their side,
Like quivers hung, and with a prelude sweet
Of charming harmony they introduce
Their sacred song, and waken raptures high;
No voice exempt, no voice but well could join
Melodious part; such concord is in Heaven.
You, Father, first they sang, omnipotent,
Immutable, immortal, infinite,
Eternal King; you, author of all being,
Fountain of light, yourself invisible
Amid the glorious brightness where you sit
Throned inaccessible, but when you shade
The full blaze of your beams, and through a cloud
Drawn round about you like a radiant shrine,
Dark with excessive bright your skirts appear,
Yet dazzle Heaven, so brightest Seraphim
Stay distant, and with both wings veil their eyes.
You next they sang, of all creation first,
Begotten Son, divine similitude,
In whose clear countenance, without a cloud
Made visible, the Almighty Father shines,
Whom else no creature can behold; on you
Impressed, the splendor of his glory abides;
Poured into you, his ample Spirit rests.
The Heaven of Heavens, and all the Powers it holds,
He made by you, and by you he threw down
The aspiring Dominations; you that day
Your Father’s dreadful thunder did not spare,
Nor stopped your flaming chariot wheels, that shook
Heaven’s everlasting frame, while on the necks
Of warring, routed angels you drove on.
Back from pursuit, your Powers with loud acclaim
Extolled you only, Son of your Father’s might,
To execute fierce vengeance on his foes.
Not so with Man: him, fallen through their malice,
Father of mercy and grace, you did not doom
So strictly, but inclined much more to pity.
No sooner did your dear and only Son
Perceive you purposed not to doom frail Man
So strictly, but inclined much more to pity,
Than he, to appease your wrath and end the strife
Of mercy and justice in your face discerned,
Regardless of the bliss in which he sat
Second to you, offered himself to die
For man’s offense. O unexampled love,
Love nowhere to be found less than divine!
Hail, Son of God, Savior of men! Your name
Shall be the copious matter of my song
Henceforth, and never shall my harp your praise
Forget, nor part it from your Father’s praise.
Thus they in Heaven, above the starry sphere,
Spent their happy hours in joy and hymning.
Meanwhile, upon the firm and opaque globe
Of this round world, whose outmost curve divides
The shining lower orbs, which it encloses,
From Chaos and the inroads of old Darkness,
Satan, alighted, walks. A globe far off
It seemed, now seems a boundless continent,
Dark, waste, and wild, under the frown of Night
Starless, exposed, and ever-threatening storms
Of Chaos blustering round, inclement sky;
Except that side which, from the wall of Heaven,
Though far away, some small reflection gains
Of glimmering air, less vexed with tempest loud.
Here walked the Fiend at large in spacious field.
As when a vulture, bred on Imaus,
Whose snowy ridge hems in the roving Tartar,
Moving away from regions scant of prey
To gorge the flesh of lambs or newborn kids
On hills where flocks are fed, flies toward the springs
Of Ganges or Hydaspes, Indian streams,
But on his way lights on the barren plains
Of Sericana, where the Chinese drive
Their light cane wagons on with sails and wind:
So on this windy sea of land the Fiend
Walked up and down alone, bent on his prey;
Alone, for in this place no other creature,
Living or lifeless, was there to be found;
None yet; but many, later, from the earth
Up here like airy vapors rose and flew,
Of all things transitory and vain, when Sin
With vanity had filled the works of men:
Both all things vain, and all who on vain things
Built foolish hopes of glory or lasting fame,
Or happiness in this life or the other;
All who have their reward on earth, the fruits
Of painful superstition and blind zeal,
Seeking nothing but the praise of men, here find
Fit retribution, empty as their deeds;
All the unfinished works of Nature’s hand,
Abortive, monstrous, mixed against their kind,
Dissolved on earth, float up here, and in vain,
Till final dissolution, wander here;
Not in the neighboring moon, as some have dreamed:
More likely dwellers hold those silver fields,
Translated saints, or middle spirits placed
Between angelic kind and human kind.
Here, born of sons and daughters badly joined,
First from the ancient world those giants came,
With many a vain exploit, though then renowned;
The builders next of Babel on the plain
Of Sennaar, and still with vain design
New Babels, if they had the means, would build;
Others came single: he who, to be thought
A god, leaped foolishly into Etna’s flames,
Empedocles; and he who, to enjoy
Plato’s Elysium, leaped into the sea,
Cleombrotus; and more too long to tell,
Embryos and idiots, hermits and friars,
White, Black, and Gray, with all their trumpery.
Here pilgrims roam, who strayed so far to seek
In Golgotha him dead who lives in Heaven;
And they who, to be sure of Paradise,
Dying put on the robes of Dominic,
Or think to pass disguised as Franciscans;
They pass the planets seven, and pass the fixed,
And that crystalline sphere whose balance weighs
The trepidation talked of, and that First Moved;
And now Saint Peter at Heaven’s wicket seems
To wait for them with keys, and at the foot
Of Heaven’s ascent they lift their feet, and then
A violent crosswind from either coast
Blows them off course ten thousand leagues awry
Into the trackless air; then you might see
Cowls, hoods, and habits, with their wearers, tossed
And fluttered into rags; then relics, beads,
Indulgences, dispensations, pardons, bulls,
The sport of winds: all these, whirled up aloft,
Fly over the world’s back side, far away,
Into a limbo, large and broad, since called
The Paradise of Fools, to few unknown
Long after, now unpeopled and untrod.
All this dark globe the Fiend found as he passed,
And long he wandered, till at last a gleam
Of dawning light turned toward it, in all haste,
His travel-weary steps. Far off he spies,
Ascending by degrees magnificent
Up to the wall of Heaven, a structure high,
Upon whose top, but far more rich, appeared
The work as of a kingly palace gate,
With frontispiece of diamond and gold
Embellished; thick with sparkling orient gems
The portal shone, inimitable on Earth
By model, or by shading pencil drawn.
The stairs were like the ones where Jacob saw
Angels ascending and descending, bands
Of shining guardians, when he fled from Esau
To Padan-aram, in the field of Luz,
Dreaming by night under the open sky,
And, waking, cried, “This is the gate of Heaven.”
Each stair was meant in mystery, nor stood
There always, but at times was drawn to Heaven
Unseen; and underneath a bright sea flowed
Of jasper, or of liquid pearl, on which
Those later come from Earth arrived by sail,
Wafted by angels, or flew across the lake
Snatched in a chariot drawn by fiery steeds.
The stairs were then let down, whether to dare
The Fiend by easy ascent, or aggravate
His sad exclusion from the doors of bliss.
Straight opposite, there opened from beneath,
Just over the blissful seat of Paradise,
A passage down to Earth, a passage wide,
Wider by far than that of later times
Over Mount Zion, and, though that was large,
Over the Promised Land, to God so dear,
By which, to visit often those glad tribes,
On high commands his angels to and fro
Passed constantly, his eye with choice regard
From Paneas, the fount of Jordan’s flood,
To Beersheba, where the Holy Land
Borders on Egypt and the Arabian shore;
So wide the opening seemed, where bounds were set
To darkness, such as bound the ocean wave.
Satan from here, now on the lower stair
That climbed by steps of gold to Heaven’s gate,
Looks down with wonder at the sudden view
Of all this world at once. As when a scout,
Through dark and desert ways with peril gone
All night, at last, by break of cheerful dawn,
Reaches the brow of some high-climbing hill,
Which to his eye discloses unaware
The goodly prospect of some foreign land
First seen, or some renowned metropolis
With glistening spires and pinnacles adorned,
Which now the rising sun gilds with his beams:
Such wonder seized, though he had looked on Heaven,
The spirit malign, but much more envy seized
At sight of all this world beheld so fair.
Round he surveys, and well he might, where he stood
So high above the circling canopy
Of Night’s extended shade; from eastern point
Of Libra to the fleecy star that bears
Andromeda far off Atlantic seas
Beyond the horizon; then from pole to pole
He views in breadth, and, without longer pause,
Straight down into the world’s first region throws
His flight precipitant, and winds with ease
Through the pure marble air his oblique way
Among innumerable stars, that shone
Stars distant, but close by seemed other worlds,
Or other worlds they seemed, or happy isles,
Like those Hesperian gardens famed of old,
Fortunate fields, and groves and flowery vales,
Thrice happy isles; but who dwelt happy there
He did not stop to ask. Above them all
The golden sun, in splendor most like Heaven,
Allured his eye. He bends his course that way
Through the calm firmament; but up or down,
By center or eccentric, hard to tell,
Or longitude, where the great luminary,
Aloof from crowded common constellations,
That from his lordly eye keep distance due,
Dispenses light from far. They, as they move
Their starry dance in numbers that compute
Days, months, and years, toward his all-cheering lamp
Turn swift their various motions, or are turned
By his magnetic beam, that gently warms
The universe, and to each inward part
With gentle penetration, though unseen,
Shoots hidden power down even to the deep:
So wondrously his shining post was set.
There lands the Fiend, a spot like which perhaps
No astronomer in the sun’s lucent orb
Through his glazed optic tube has ever seen.
The place he found beyond expression bright,
Compared with all on Earth, metal or stone;
Not all its parts alike, but all suffused
With radiant light, as glowing iron with fire;
If metal, part seemed gold, part silver clear;
If stone, carbuncle most, or chrysolite,
Ruby or topaz, to the twelve that shone
In Aaron’s breastplate, and a stone besides
More often pictured in the mind than seen,
That stone, or one like that which here below
Philosophers in vain so long have sought,
In vain, though by their powerful art they bind
Volatile Hermes, and call up unbound
In various shapes old Proteus from the sea,
Drained through an alembic to his native form.
What wonder, then, if fields and regions here
Breathe forth pure elixir, and rivers run
Drinkable gold, when with one potent touch
The arch-chemist Sun, so far from us remote,
Produces, mixed with moisture of the earth,
Here in the dark so many precious things
Of color glorious and effect so rare?
Here the Devil met new matter for his gaze,
Undazzled; far and wide his eye commands,
For sight no obstacle found here, nor shade,
But all sunshine, as when his beams at noon
Culminate from the equator, as they now
Shot upward, straight, so that on no side round
Can shadow fall from opaque body; the air,
Nowhere so clear, sharpened his visual ray
To objects far away, by which he soon
Saw within sight a glorious angel stand,
The same whom John saw also in the sun.
His back was turned, but not his brightness hid;
Of beaming sunny rays, a golden crown
Circled his head, nor less his locks behind,
Lustrous, upon his shoulders fledged with wings
Lay waving round. On some great charge employed
He seemed, or fixed in contemplation deep.
Glad was the spirit impure, as now in hope
To find who might direct his wandering flight
To Paradise, the happy seat of Man,
His journey’s end and our beginning woe.
But first he means to change his own true shape,
Which else might work him danger or delay;
And now a stripling cherub he appears,
Not of the first, yet such that in his face
Youth smiled celestial, and to every limb
Suitable grace diffused, so well he feigned;
Under a coronet his flowing hair
In curls on either cheek played; wings he wore
Of many a colored plume sprinkled with gold;
His garment girded up for speed; and held
Before his graceful steps a silver wand.
He did not come unheard; the angel bright,
Before he came close, turned his radiant face,
Warned by his hearing, and at once was known
The archangel Uriel, one of the seven
Who in God’s presence, nearest to his throne,
Stand ready at command, and are his eyes
That run through all the heavens, or down to Earth
Bear his swift errands over wet and dry,
Through sea and land; and Satan hails him so:
“Uriel, since you, of the seven who stand
In sight of God’s high throne, gloriously bright,
Are first to bear his great authentic will,
As his interpreter, through highest Heaven,
Where all his sons attend your embassy;
And here are likeliest, by supreme decree,
Like honor to obtain, and, as his eye,
To visit often this new creation round;
Unspeakable desire to see and know
All these his wondrous works, but chiefly Man,
His chief delight and favor, him for whom
All these his works so wondrous he ordained,
Has brought me from the choirs of Cherubim
Alone thus wandering. Brightest Seraph, tell
In which of all these shining orbs has Man
His settled home, or settled home has none,
But all these shining orbs his choice to dwell;
That I may find him, and with secret gaze
Or open admiration look on him
On whom the great Creator has bestowed
Worlds, and on whom has poured out all these graces;
That both in him and all things, as is fit,
The universal Maker we may praise;
Who justly has driven out his rebel foes
To deepest Hell, and to repair that loss
Created this new happy race of men
To serve him better: wise are all his ways.”
So spoke the false dissembler, unperceived;
For neither man nor angel can discern
Hypocrisy, the only evil that walks
Invisible, except to God alone,
By his permissive will, through Heaven and Earth;
Often, though wisdom wakes, suspicion sleeps
At wisdom’s gate, and to simplicity
Resigns her charge, while goodness thinks no ill
Where no ill seems; which now, for once, beguiled
Uriel, though regent of the sun, and held
The sharpest-sighted spirit of all in Heaven;
Who to the fraudulent impostor foul,
In his uprightness, gave this answer back:
“Fair angel, your desire, which tends to know
The works of God, thereby to glorify
The great Work-Master, leads to no excess
That earns rebuke, but rather merits praise
The more it seems excess, that led you here
From your empyreal mansion thus alone,
To witness with your eyes what some, perhaps
Content with hearsay, only hear in Heaven:
For wonderful indeed are all his works,
Pleasant to know, and worthiest to be all
Held in remembrance always with delight;
But what created mind can comprehend
Their number, or the wisdom infinite
That brought them forth, but hid their causes deep?
I saw when at his word the formless mass,
This world’s material mold, came to a heap:
Confusion heard his voice, and wild uproar
Stood ruled, stood vast infinitude confined;
Till at his second bidding darkness fled,
Light shone, and order from disorder sprang:
Swift to their several quarters hastened then
The cumbrous elements, earth, flood, air, fire;
And this ethereal quintessence of Heaven
Flew upward, spirited with various forms,
That rolled in circles, and were turned to stars
Numberless, as you see, and how they move;
Each had its place appointed, each its course;
The rest, in circuit, walls this universe.
Look downward on that globe, whose nearer side
With light from here, though but reflected, shines;
That place is Earth, the seat of Man; that light
His day, which else, as the other hemisphere,
Night would invade; but there the neighboring moon
(So call that opposite fair star) her aid
Timely interposes, and her monthly round
Still ending, still renewing, through mid-Heaven,
With borrowed light her countenance triform
Hence fills and empties to enlighten the Earth,
And in her pale dominion checks the night.
That spot to which I point is Paradise,
Adam’s abode; those lofty shades, his bower.
Your way you cannot miss; my own calls me.”
This said, he turned; and Satan, bowing low,
As is the way in Heaven with higher spirits,
Where honor due and reverence none neglects,
Took leave, and toward the coast of Earth beneath,
Down from the ecliptic, sped with hoped success,
Throws his steep flight in many an airy wheel,
Nor paused till on Niphates’ top he lights.

blocks.p: Hail, holy Light (1). Milton, by now wholly blind, invokes light itself, echoing “God is light” [1 John 1:5] and the light no one can approach [1 Tim. 6:16].
Stygian pool (14). Hell, named from the Styx, river of the classical underworld; Books I and II were set there and in Chaos.
utter and ... middle darkness (16). “Utter” means outer: the outer darkness of Hell and the middle darkness of Chaos.
Orphic lyre (17). Orpheus, the mythic singer who went down to the underworld; a hymn to Night was ascribed to him.
drop serene ... dim suffusion (25). Gutta serena and suffusio, medical names in Milton’s day for kinds of blindness.
Zion (30). The holy hill of Jerusalem, here standing for Scripture and its sacred poetry beside the Muses’ classical haunts.
Thamyris ... Maeonides (35). Thamyris, a Thracian bard blinded by the Muses; Maeonides is Homer, by tradition blind.
Tiresias and Phineus (36). Blind prophets of Greek legend, of Thebes and of Thrace.
numbers ... the wakeful bird (38). “Numbers” are verses; the bird is the nightingale, which sings in the dark.
Empyrean (57). The highest heaven, the region of pure fire and light.
reason also is choice (108). Milton held that to reason is itself to choose; without freedom, reason too is idle.
devoted (208). In the old sense: set apart for destruction, as the Latin sacer and devotus.
silence was in Heaven (218). [Rev. 8:1].
unprevented (231). Not anticipated by any request: grace comes before it is asked or sought.
Imputed (291). Credited to them: the Son’s merit is counted as theirs.
Equal to God ... quitted all (306). Echoes the Son’s self-emptying and exaltation [Phil. 2:6–9].
Thrones, Princedoms, Powers, Dominions (320). Orders of angels [Col. 1:16]; the bowing of every knee follows [Phil. 2:10].
all in all ... all you gods (341). [1 Cor. 15:28]; “gods” here means the angels, as in [Ps. 97:7].
amaranth (352). From the Greek for “unfading,” a legendary flower that never withers [1 Pet. 5:4].
Dark with excessive bright ... skirts (380). Brightness so intense it looks dark; “skirts” are the hem of a robe [Exod. 33:22–23].
Imaus (431). In ancient geography, the mountain range of central Asia (the Himalaya and its western extension).
Hydaspes ... Sericana (436). The Hydaspes is the Jhelum in the Punjab; Sericana, northern China, where travelers reported wagons driven by sails.
Translated saints (461). Those taken bodily into heaven without dying, as Enoch and Elijah.
giants ... Sennaar (464). The giants of [Gen. 6:4]; Sennaar is Shinar, the plain of Babel [Gen. 11:2].
Empedocles ... Cleombrotus (471). Empedocles leapt into Etna to vanish and be thought a god; Cleombrotus drowned himself after reading Plato’s Phaedo.
White, Black, and Gray (475). Carmelite, Dominican, and Franciscan friars, named by the colors of their habits.
robes of Dominic ... Franciscans (479). Some had themselves buried in friars’ habits, hoping to slip into heaven.
crystalline sphere ... First Moved (482). Outer spheres of Ptolemaic astronomy; “trepidation” was a supposed wobble of the heavens, and the First Moved (Primum Mobile) the outermost sphere.
dispensations, pardons, bulls (492). Papal exemptions from church law, remissions of penance, and papal decrees, named for their seals (bullae).
Jacob (510). His dream of the ladder at Luz, which he renamed Bethel [Gen. 28:12–19].
chariot drawn by fiery steeds (522). The ascent of Elijah [2 Kings 2:11].
Paneas ... Beersheba (535). The northern and southern bounds of the Holy Land; Paneas lies at a source of the Jordan.
Libra ... Andromeda (558). From Libra in the east to Aries, the Ram (“the fleecy star”), with Andromeda above it over the western Atlantic.
glazed optic tube (590). The telescope, through which Galileo and others had recently observed sunspots.
Aaron’s breastplate (598). The high priest’s breastplate set with twelve stones [Exod. 28:15–21]; “that stone” is the alchemists’ philosophers’ stone.
Volatile Hermes ... Proteus ... alembic (603). Alchemical terms: Hermes is quicksilver, Proteus is shape-shifting matter, an alembic is a still.
elixir ... drinkable gold (607). The elixir of life and aurum potabile, a gold medicine; the sun was thought to ripen metals and gems underground.
whom John saw ... in the sun (623). [Rev. 19:17].
Uriel (648). “Light of God,” one of the seven archangels of Jewish tradition [Zech. 4:10; Rev. 8:2].
Niphates (742). A mountain range in Armenia, near the traditional site of Eden.
